Supreme Court’s Next Move? Fifth Circuit Blocks Use of 1798 Alien Enemies Act By [Your Name/News Organization]
Febuary 29, 2024 – Washington, D.C.
WASHINGTON – Judges on the Federal Court of appeals for the Fifth Circuit have blocked the use of a 1798 law, the Alien Enemies Act, to expel Venezuelan migrants. The court found no evidence of an “invasion” or “predatory incursion” as required by the statute.
Migrant Expulsion Blocked Under 1798 Law Federal judges reject Trump administration’s attempt to use wartime statute against Venezuelan migrants.
The Fifth Circuit’s decision is a blow to efforts to use the Alien Enemies Act for immigration enforcement. Previous lower court rulings had also opposed the law’s application in this context. The Supreme Court may yet weigh in on the core issue of the law’s applicability. The Biden administration’s stance on national security authorities remains a point of contention. The Supreme Court has yet to rule on the central question of the Alien Enemies Act’s legitimate use in this context. Though,it is indeed highly probable that the Department of Justice will appeal the Fifth Circuit’s decision. This appeal could lead to the case being presented to the Supreme Court for a final ruling.
A White House spokesperson,Abigail Jackson,responded to the ruling,stating,”The authority to conduct national security operations in defense of the United States and to remove terrorists belongs exclusively to the president.” The statement maintained that Trump exercised legitimate authority using the Alien Enemies Act to expel U.S. enemies, including members of the TDA gang.
The Trump administration’s assertion that the gang’s actions constituted an “invasion” directed by Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro had also been questioned by U.S. intelligence agencies. Furthermore, lawyers for several targeted migrants contested the government’s efforts to classify them as gang members. Reports indicate that over 250 individuals expelled and deported were later released and repatriated to Venezuela.
While not the final word on the case, the Fifth Circuit’s decision represents a notable setback for Trump’s immigration agenda and a victory for his opponents. Lee Gelerner, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union who represented Venezuelan citizens held in North Texas, commented on the ruling.
“The attempt by the Trump administration to use a war law in peacetime for immigration purposes has been correctly struck down by the Court,” Gelerner stated. “This sentence clarifies that the courts exist to maintain executive power within the legal limits, and that even the president cannot simply declare the state of emergency whenever it suits him
